trap.wrong: "Store latitude and longitude, add an index on each, and compute distance for every row."
trap.why: Separate indexes on lat and lng don't answer 'near' efficiently, and computing distance to every row doesn't scale. Spatial indexing (geohash, quadtree, S2/H3, R-tree) narrows candidates first.
trap.probe: Whether you know spatial indexes, cell edge effects, and how to handle fast-moving points.
trap.say: "I'd index by spatial cells (geohash, S2 or H3), query the target cell plus its neighbours, then compute exact distances on that small candidate set; for moving drivers, keep locations in memory keyed by cell."

thesis: Spatial queries need a spatial index that groups nearby points: geohash prefixes, quadtrees, Google S2 or Uber H3 cells, or R-trees (PostGIS). Query the relevant cells and neighbours to get candidates, then rank by exact distance. Fast-moving points need an in-memory, frequently updated index.
pitch: Latitude and longitude indexes separately give you a band, not a circle, so the database still scans lots of rows. Spatial indexes map 2D locations into cells. Geohash encodes a location as a string where a shared prefix means nearby, so a prefix range query finds candidates; but two close points can sit on opposite sides of a cell boundary, so you always search neighbouring cells too. S2 and H3 provide hierarchical cells with better shape properties; H3's hexagons have uniform neighbours, which suits ride-hailing and delivery. For static data like stores, PostGIS with an R-tree (GiST) index handles 'within radius' and 'nearest' queries well. For moving drivers updating every few seconds, I'd keep current locations in memory, such as Redis GEO commands or a sharded in-memory index keyed by cell, rather than writing every update to a disk-based database.

points.d: Two B-tree indexes can't efficiently answer a 2D proximity query; you end up scanning a large band and computing distance per row.
Geohash, S2 and H3 map points to cells at chosen resolutions. Nearby points mostly share cells or prefixes.
Points near a cell edge have nearest neighbours in adjacent cells. Query the cell plus surrounding cells, then filter by exact distance.
R-trees (PostGIS GiST) and quadtrees index shapes and points directly; good for static or slowly changing data and complex geometry.
Dense cities need finer cells; rural areas need coarser cells or expanding-ring searches until enough candidates are found.
Frequent location updates belong in an in-memory index (Redis GEO, custom sharded grid), with periodic persistence for history.

decision: Static places: PostGIS or a search engine with geo support. High-frequency moving objects: in-memory cell index (H3 or geohash) sharded by region. Always query neighbours and refine with exact distance.
numbers: Driver updates: 500,000 active drivers updating every 4 seconds is 125,000 writes/s, too many for a typical relational primary but fine for a sharded in-memory index.
Geohash precision: 6 characters is roughly a 1.2 km × 0.6 km cell; 7 characters roughly 150 m.
pitfalls: Searching only the user's own cell and missing closer points across the boundary.
Using one cell size for dense cities and empty regions.
Writing every location ping to the main database.
Forgetting that longitude distance shrinks toward the poles when doing naive math.

followups.q: How do you find the K nearest when nearby cells are empty?
followups.a: Expanding-ring search: widen to neighbouring rings of cells until you have at least K candidates, then rank.
Each hexagon has six equidistant neighbours, which makes distance-based ring searches and aggregation more uniform.

followups.q: How do you shard a geospatial index?
followups.a: By coarse region or cell prefix, with hot cities split further; keep queries near borders able to hit adjacent shards.

example: A delivery app keeps courier locations in Redis keyed by H3 cells at resolution 8 and queries the order's cell plus one ring of neighbours, ranking about 50 candidates by road-network ETA. Store locations live in PostGIS for radius searches.
